blocks.html: In Points, Lines, Segments and Rays you learned to name points, lines, segments and rays by looking at them. Geometry now builds a careful system out of those same ideas. A few words stay undefined, a few basic facts are accepted as starting points, and every other word and fact is built from those.

A point marks a location and has no size. A line is perfectly straight, has no thickness, and goes on forever in both directions. A plane is a flat surface that goes on forever. We describe these instead of defining them, because a definition has to use simpler words, and these are the simplest we have.

blocks.html: A postulate is a statement we accept without proof, the way a building rests on its foundation. Through any two points there is exactly one line. Two different lines meet in at most one point. Three points that are not on one line lie in exactly one plane. If two points lie in a plane, the whole line through them does too. Two planes that meet, meet in a line. Every theorem later in this course rests on short chains of facts like these.
Segment Addition Postulate: if $B$ is between $A$ and $C$ on a segment, then $AB + BC = AC$. The two parts add up to the whole.

steps: $Q$ is between $P$ and $R$, so $PQ + QR = PR$.

blocks.html: Trusting the picture. A sketch may make two segments look equal, or two lines look parallel, but a drawing is never exact. From an unmarked diagram you may assume only how points sit: which points are on a line, which point is between two others, and where lines cross. Equal lengths, equal angles, right angles and parallel lines must be given (in words or with tick marks, arcs and arrows) or proved.
Notation matters: $\overline{AB}$ is the segment, and $AB$ (no bar) is its length. You can add lengths, but not segments.

blocks.html: In Distance Between Two Points you found the distance between two points by drawing a right triangle under the segment and using the Pythagorean theorem. In Points, Lines and Planes you met $AB$ as the length of a segment. Here we turn that picture into a formula, and add a second one for the point exactly halfway between, the midpoint.

Distance. From $A(x_1, y_1)$ to $B(x_2, y_2)$, walk across $x_2 - x_1$ and up $y_2 - y_1$. Those are the legs of a right triangle and $\overline{AB}$ is the hypotenuse, so $AB^2 = (x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2$. Squaring also takes care of direction: a step of $-4$ and a step of $4$ both give $16$.
Midpoint. Halfway along the segment, you have gone half of the way across and half of the way up. Half of the way from $x_1$ to $x_2$ lands on their average, $\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$; the same is true for $y$.
$$AB = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$$ $$M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$$ The distance is the Pythagorean theorem; the midpoint is the average of the endpoints.

blocks.name: geoboard
blocks.cap: Drag $A$ or $B$. The length updates, and $M$ stays exactly halfway, at the average of the coordinates.

blocks.title: An exact distance
blocks.q: Find the distance between $A(-2, 3)$ and $B(4, -1)$.

blocks.title: A midpoint
blocks.q: Find the midpoint of the segment from $A(-3, 5)$ to $B(7, -2)$.
steps: $M = \left(2, \frac{3}{2}\right)$. Check: it lies between the endpoints in both directions.

blocks.title: Working backward to an endpoint
blocks.q: $M(1, -2)$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ and $A = (-4, 3)$. Find $B$.
steps: From $A$ to $M$: $x$ goes up by $1 - (-4) = 5$ and $y$ goes down by $3 - (-2) = 5$.
$M$ is halfway, so repeat the same step from $M$: $B = (1 + 5, -2 - 5) = (6, -7)$.

blocks.html: Two slips to watch for. (1) Subtracting for a midpoint: $\frac{x_2 - x_1}{2}$ is half of the change, not a location. Check: the midpoint must lie between the two endpoints. (2) Dropping the sign before squaring: $(-4)^2 = 16$, not $-16$. Check: the distance is always at least as big as the larger of the two changes.

blocks.html: An angle is two rays that share an endpoint, called the vertex. You know angle pairs from Complementary, Supplementary and Vertical Angles; now we name and measure angles with the same care we used for segments in Points, Lines and Planes.

items: Name an angle by three points with the vertex in the middle: $\angle ABC$ has its vertex at $B$. Use one letter, $\angle B$, only when no other angle shares that vertex.
$\angle ABC$ is the figure; $m\angle ABC$ is its measure in degrees. Two angles are congruent ($\angle A \cong \angle B$) exactly when their measures are equal.
Acute: less than $90^\circ$. Right: $90^\circ$. Obtuse: between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. Straight: $180^\circ$.

blocks.html: Measuring an angle is like reading a ruler that has been bent into a half circle. A protractor places ray $BA$ at one reading and ray $BC$ at another; the measure is the difference. If ray $BD$ lies between them, its reading is in the middle, so the two smaller differences add to the big one. That is the Angle Addition Postulate, the angle version of segment addition.

If $D$ is in the interior of $\angle ABC$, then $m\angle ABD + m\angle DBC = m\angle ABC$. A ray $\overrightarrow{BD}$ bisects $\angle ABC$ when it splits it into two congruent angles, each half of the whole.

blocks.name: geoboard
blocks.cap: Drag $D$. The two angle measures always add to $m\angle ABC$. When they are equal, $\overrightarrow{BD}$ is the bisector.

blocks.title: Angle addition
blocks.q: $D$ is in the interior of $\angle ABC$, $m\angle ABC = 112^\circ$ and $m\angle ABD = 47^\circ$. Find $m\angle DBC$.
steps: By the Angle Addition Postulate, ${}47 + m\angle DBC = 112$.

blocks.title: A bisector with algebra
blocks.q: $\overrightarrow{BD}$ bisects $\angle ABC$, $m\angle ABD = (4x + 6)^\circ$ and $m\angle DBC = (6x - 20)^\circ$. Find $m\angle ABC$.
steps: A bisector makes two congruent angles: $4x + 6 = 6x - 20$.

blocks.html: Answering with $x$ when the question asks for an angle. In the example, $x = 13$ is only a stepping stone; the angle is $116^\circ$. Reread the question before you write the answer. Another slip: naming an angle $\angle BAC$ when the vertex is $B$. The middle letter must be the vertex.

blocks.html: A construction uses only two tools. The compass draws circles and arcs; the straightedge draws lines but has no marks for measuring. Greek geometers chose these tools on purpose: with no ruler or protractor, every result has to come from reasoning, not reading a scale. You will use the angle ideas from Angles and Angle Bisectors.

Every construction rests on one fact: all points on an arc are the same distance from its center. So a compass copies a length exactly. Equal lengths then give triangles with three matching sides, and triangles with three matching sides are congruent (SSS, which you will prove in SSS, SAS and ASA). Congruent triangles have matching angles. That is why the steps work, not just how to do them.

blocks.name: geo-construct
blocks.cap: Copying a segment: the compass carries the length $AB$ to the ray.

blocks.title: Copy an angle
blocks.q: Copy $\angle A$ so that the copy opens from a ray that starts at $D$.
steps: With the compass on $A$, draw an arc that crosses both sides of the angle at $P$ and $Q$.
Keep the width. With the compass on $D$, draw the same arc, crossing the ray at $R$.
Set the compass to the distance $PQ$. With it on $R$, mark $S$ where it crosses the arc.
Draw ray $DS$. Triangles $APQ$ and $DRS$ have $AP = DR$, $AQ = DS$ and $PQ = RS$, so they are congruent by SSS, and $\angle D \cong \angle A$.
blocks.a: Ray $DS$ makes an angle congruent to $\angle A$.

blocks.name: geo-construct
blocks.cap: Bisecting an angle, step by step. Press Next to draw each arc.

blocks.title: Bisect an angle
blocks.q: Bisect $\angle A$, and explain why the two halves are equal.
steps: With the compass on $A$, draw an arc crossing the sides at $P$ and $Q$, so $AP = AQ$.
Open the compass to more than half of $PQ$. Draw an arc from $P$ and, with the same width, an arc from $Q$. They cross at $X$, so $PX = QX$.
Draw ray $AX$. Triangles $APX$ and $AQX$ share side $AX$, so they are congruent by SSS.
Matching angles of congruent triangles are equal: $\angle PAX \cong \angle QAX$.

blocks.html: To bisect a segment, draw equal arcs from both endpoints above and below it; the line through the two crossings cuts the segment in half at a right angle. You will study it in Constructing Perpendicular and Parallel Lines.

blocks.name: geo-construct
blocks.cap: Bisecting segment $AB$: the line through the arc crossings passes through the midpoint $M$.

blocks.html: A compass copies lengths; a straightedge draws lines. To copy a segment or angle, or to bisect one, use arcs of equal radius, and the result is exact because it creates congruent triangles.

Changing the compass width partway through. The bisector works only because $PX = QX$; if you widen the compass between the two arcs, $PX \ne QX$ and the ray misses the true bisector. Check: keep the compass hinge firm, and if the two halves do not look equal, redraw the arcs.

blocks.name: geo-construct
blocks.cap: The mistake on purpose: with two different widths, the ray splits the angle unevenly.

blocks.html: With the moves from Copying and Bisecting with Compass and Straightedge you can also build right angles and parallel lines. Each construction is a short chain: arcs make equal distances, and equal distances force the lines into place.

Look at the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$. Arcs of the same radius from $A$ and from $B$ cross at $X$ and $Y$, so $X$ is the same distance from $A$ as from $B$, and so is $Y$. The points that are equally far from $A$ and $B$ form exactly one line, the perpendicular bisector (you will prove this in Perpendicular Bisectors and the Circumcenter). Two points fix a line, so line $XY$ must be it.

blocks.name: geo-construct
blocks.cap: The perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$: equal arcs from both ends.

blocks.html: If $P$ is not on line $\ell$, draw an arc centered at $P$ that crosses $\ell$ at $A$ and $B$. Now $P$ is equally far from $A$ and $B$, so the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$ passes through $P$. Construct it as before.

blocks.name: geo-construct
blocks.cap: Dropping a perpendicular from $P$ to the line.

blocks.title: A perpendicular at a point on the line
blocks.q: $P$ lies on line $\ell$. Construct the line through $P$ perpendicular to $\ell$.
steps: With the compass on $P$, mark $A$ and $B$ on $\ell$, one on each side, so $PA = PB$.
Open the compass wider. Draw arcs from $A$ and from $B$ (same width) that cross at $X$.
Draw line $PX$. Both $P$ and $X$ are equally far from $A$ and $B$, so $PX$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$: it meets $\ell$ at a right angle at $P$.

blocks.html: To draw the line through $P$ parallel to $\ell$, draw any line through $P$ crossing $\ell$ at $Q$. Then copy the angle at $Q$ to $P$, in the same position. The two angles are corresponding angles, and congruent corresponding angles make the lines parallel (the converse you will prove in Proving Theorems about Lines and Angles).

blocks.name: geo-construct
blocks.cap: The parallel construction copies a corresponding angle.

blocks.html: The perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$ is the set of points equally far from $A$ and $B$, so equal arcs from $A$ and $B$ find it. A parallel line comes from copying a corresponding angle.

blocks.title: Checking with coordinates
blocks.q: Find the slope of the perpendicular bisector of $A(1, 1)$ and $B(7, 5)$, and the point it must pass through.
steps: Slope of $\overline{AB}$: $\frac{5 - 1}{7 - 1} = \frac{2}{3}$. A perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal: $-\frac{3}{2}$.

blocks.html: Drawing the first arc from $P$ too small. If it touches line $\ell$ once or not at all, there is no segment $\overline{AB}$ to bisect. Open the compass wide enough to cross $\ell$ twice, and keep one width for each pair of arcs.

blocks.html: A polygon is inscribed in a circle when all its vertices lie on the circle. Using the constructions from Constructing Perpendicular and Parallel Lines, you can inscribe three regular polygons exactly: a hexagon, an equilateral triangle and a square.

Keep the compass at the radius $r$ and mark a point $B$ on the circle, one compass width from $A$. Triangle $OAB$ has $OA = OB = r$ (radii) and $AB = r$ (the compass), so it is equilateral and its angle at $O$ is $60^\circ$. Six such steps use $6 \cdot 60^\circ = 360^\circ$, exactly once around, so you land back on $A$ with six equal sides.

blocks.name: geo-construct
blocks.cap: Stepping around the circle with the radius makes a regular hexagon.

items: Hexagon: step around the circle with the radius as the compass width; connect the six points. Each side equals $r$.
Equilateral triangle: make the hexagon's points, then connect every other one. Each side skips one $60^\circ$ step, so each central angle is $120^\circ$.
Square: draw a diameter, construct the diameter perpendicular to it, and connect the four endpoints. The central angles are $90^\circ$ each.

blocks.name: geo-construct
blocks.cap: Two perpendicular diameters give an inscribed square.

blocks.html: A regular polygon with $n$ sides, inscribed in a circle, has $n$ equal central angles of $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$. Constructions produce those angles: $60^\circ$ by stepping with the radius, $120^\circ$ by skipping a point, $90^\circ$ with perpendicular diameters.

blocks.title: The side of the inscribed square
blocks.q: A square is inscribed in a circle of radius $6$. How long is each side?
steps: Two radii to neighboring corners meet at a right angle, since the diagonals are perpendicular diameters.
The side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $6$ and $6$: $\sqrt{6^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}$.

blocks.title: The inscribed equilateral triangle
blocks.q: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle of radius $4$. Find its perimeter.
steps: Draw radii to two vertices and the perpendicular from the center to the side between them. The central angle $120^\circ$ is split into two $60^\circ$ angles.
In the $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle with hypotenuse $4$, half of the side is opposite $60^\circ$: $2\sqrt{3}$. So each side is $4\sqrt{3}$.

blocks.html: You will meet the $30$-$60$-$90$ ratios properly in 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 Triangles; here it is enough to see that the side comes from a right triangle.

blocks.html: Geometry states almost every fact as an if-then sentence, called a conditional: If $p$, then $q$. The part after "if" is the hypothesis; the part after "then" is the conclusion. You already know the words point, line and plane from Points, Lines and Planes; now we look at how sentences about them fit together.

A conditional is false in only one situation: the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false. So a single counterexample is enough to show a conditional is false. To show it is true, you need a reason that covers every case.

head: Form
Pattern
Example
True?
rows: If an angle measures $30^\circ$, then it is acute.
If an angle is acute, then it measures $30^\circ$.
If an angle does not measure $30^\circ$, then it is not acute.
If an angle is not acute, then it does not measure $30^\circ$.
blocks.cap: The four related conditionals. Converse swaps; inverse negates; contrapositive does both.

blocks.html: Picture all the things where $p$ is true as a circle sitting inside a bigger circle of things where $q$ is true. "If $p$, then $q$" says the $p$ circle is inside the $q$ circle. Then anything outside the $q$ circle is also outside the $p$ circle: that is the contrapositive, and it must be true too. But a point can be in the $q$ circle without being in the $p$ circle, so the converse can fail.

blocks.name: geo-fig
blocks.cap: "If $p$, then $q$": the $p$ circle sits inside the $q$ circle. A $45^\circ$ angle is acute but not $30^\circ$, so the converse fails.

opts.label: A circle for p inside a bigger circle for q

blocks.html: A statement and its contrapositive are always both true or both false. The converse and the inverse match each other, but not necessarily the statement. When a statement and its converse are both true, combine them into a biconditional: $p$ if and only if $q$.

blocks.title: Writing the related conditionals
blocks.q: Write the converse, inverse and contrapositive of: If two angles are vertical angles, then they are congruent. Which are true?
steps: Converse: If two angles are congruent, then they are vertical angles. False: two $40^\circ$ angles in different places are congruent but not vertical.
Inverse: If two angles are not vertical angles, then they are not congruent. False, by the same example.
Contrapositive: If two angles are not congruent, then they are not vertical angles. True, because the statement is true.
blocks.a: Only the contrapositive is true (along with the statement).

blocks.title: A counterexample
blocks.q: Show that this is false: If $x^2 = 49$, then $x = 7$.
steps: We need a value that makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false.

blocks.title: A biconditional
blocks.q: Can If an angle is a right angle, then it measures $90^\circ$ be written as a biconditional?
steps: The converse is If an angle measures $90^\circ$, then it is a right angle, which is also true.
Both directions hold, so: An angle is a right angle if and only if it measures $90^\circ$.
blocks.a: Yes. Every good definition works in both directions like this.

blocks.html: Assuming the converse is true because the statement is. "If a figure is a square, then it has four right angles" is true, but its converse, "If a figure has four right angles, then it is a square," is false: a $3 \times 5$ rectangle is a counterexample. Before you use a converse, look for a counterexample.

blocks.html: In Why Each Step Keeps the Balance you saw that each step of solving an equation keeps the balance. A geometry proof asks you to name the rule behind each step. The rules are the properties of equality, and they work the same way for lengths and angle measures as for $x$. They are reliable for the reasons you met in If-Then Statements: each one is an if-then statement that is always true.

head: Property
If…
then…
blocks.cap: The properties of equality used as reasons. They also hold for congruence: $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AB}$ (reflexive), and so on.

blocks.html: Each property says: if two quantities are equal, then doing the same thing to both keeps them equal. A balance that is level stays level when you add the same weight to both pans. That is why a solution found this way is guaranteed, not just likely.

blocks.name: balance
blocks.cap: Do the same thing to both sides and the scale stays level. That is the Subtraction and Division Properties at work.

blocks.html: Write each step of a solution with the property that justifies it. Undoing addition uses the Subtraction Property, undoing multiplication uses the Division Property, and replacing a quantity with an equal one is Substitution.

blocks.title: Solving with reasons
blocks.q: Solve $3(x - 4) = 2x + 1$ and justify each step.

blocks.title: Angles instead of $x$
blocks.q: $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ are complementary, and $m\angle 1 = 35^\circ$. Justify finding $m\angle 2$.

blocks.html: Mixing up the Symmetric and Transitive Properties. Symmetric only swaps the two sides of one equation ($AB = CD$, so $CD = AB$). Transitive links two equations through a shared middle ($a = b$ and $b = c$, so $a = c$). Also, "combine like terms" simplifies one side; it is not a property of equality, since nothing is done to both sides.

blocks.html: A proof is a chain of statements. Each statement must follow from the given information or from earlier statements, and each one needs a reason. You have the pieces: definitions (like midpoint and bisector from Angles and Angle Bisectors), postulates, and the properties of equality from Properties of Equality as Reasons.

items: Allowed reasons: given information, definitions, postulates, properties of equality and congruence, and theorems you have already proved.
Not allowed: "it looks that way," measuring the picture, or the statement you are trying to prove.

blocks.html: A drawing shows one case; a proof covers every case at once. If you measure a diagram and find two angles equal, you know about that drawing. If you prove it, you know it for every figure that fits the given facts, however it is drawn.

Work from both ends. Write the given facts at the top and the goal at the bottom. Ask: what definition or theorem would give me the goal? What would I need for that? Keep going until the two ends meet. Then write it neatly, top to bottom.

blocks.title: A two-column proof
blocks.q: Given: $M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$. Prove: $AM = \frac{1}{2}AB$.
steps: 4. $AM + AM = AB$ — Substitution Property (step 2 into step 3).
blocks.a: Each step follows from the ones above it, so $AM = \frac{1}{2}AB$.

blocks.name: angle
blocks.cap: Two angles that fill a right angle always add to $90^\circ$. The next example proves it.

blocks.title: A paragraph proof
blocks.q: Given: $\angle ABC$ is a right angle and $D$ is in its interior. Prove: $\angle ABD$ and $\angle DBC$ are complementary.
steps: Because $\angle ABC$ is a right angle, $m\angle ABC = 90^\circ$ by the definition of a right angle.
$D$ is in the interior, so the Angle Addition Postulate gives $m\angle ABD + m\angle DBC = m\angle ABC$.
Two angles whose measures add to $90^\circ$ are complementary, by definition.
blocks.a: The same reasoning in sentences: a paragraph proof is just as valid as a two-column one.

blocks.html: Every statement in a proof needs a reason that comes from the given facts, a definition, a postulate, a property, or a theorem already proved. Plan from both ends, then write from the top down.

Using what you are trying to prove as a reason, or trusting the diagram. "The angles are equal because they look equal" and "because that is what we want to show" both prove nothing. Check each reason: could you point to the given fact, definition or theorem it comes from?

blocks.html: In Parallel Lines Cut by a Transversal you saw that parallel lines cut by a transversal make pairs of equal angles. Now you will prove those facts with the tools from Writing a Proof, and also prove their converses, which run the other way.

Vertical Angles Theorem: vertical angles are congruent. Proof: When two lines cross, $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ form a linear pair, so $m\angle 1 + m\angle 2 = 180^\circ$. Also $\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$ form a linear pair, so $m\angle 2 + m\angle 3 = 180^\circ$. By substitution $m\angle 1 + m\angle 2 = m\angle 2 + m\angle 3$, and subtracting $m\angle 2$ gives $m\angle 1 = m\angle 3$.

We accept one fact about parallel lines as a postulate: if two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, corresponding angles are congruent, along with its converse. Everything else follows. For example, an alternate interior angle is vertical to a corresponding angle, so it is congruent too: the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem is two short steps from the postulate.

blocks.name: angle
blocks.cap: Drag the transversal and switch between the pairs. With parallel lines, each pair is either congruent or supplementary.

head: Pair
Where the angles sit
With parallel lines
rows: between the lines, opposite sides of the transversal
blocks.cap: Angle pairs formed by two parallel lines and a transversal.

blocks.title: Proving the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem
blocks.q: Given: $\ell \parallel m$, cut by transversal $t$. Prove: $\angle 3 \cong \angle 6$ (alternate interior angles).
steps: 2. $\angle 2 \cong \angle 6$ — Corresponding Angles Postulate (both are above their line, right of $t$).

blocks.title: Using a converse
blocks.q: Now suppose we do not know whether $\ell \parallel m$. In the same numbering, $m\angle 3 = (5x - 12)^\circ$ and $m\angle 6 = (3x + 20)^\circ$. For what $x$ is $\ell \parallel m$?
steps: If alternate interior angles are congruent, the lines are parallel (the converse). So set them equal: $5x - 12 = 3x + 20$.

blocks.title: An angle chase
blocks.q: $\ell \parallel m$ and $m\angle 1 = 118^\circ$. Find $m\angle 6$.
blocks.a: $62^\circ$. The angles $\angle 1$ and $\angle 6$ are not one of the named pairs, so the chase took two steps.

blocks.html: Parallel lines give congruent corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles, and supplementary same-side interior angles. The converses say the reverse: if one of those angle facts holds, the lines are parallel.

Running the logic backward. To prove two lines are parallel, you cannot use "parallel lines make congruent alternate interior angles": that assumes what you want. Use the converse: "if alternate interior angles are congruent, then the lines are parallel." Check by asking which part you know (angles or lines) and which part you want.

blocks.html: In Function Notation, a function takes an input and gives exactly one output. A transformation is a function whose inputs and outputs are points: it sends each point $P$ of the plane to an image point $T(P)$, usually written $P'$. The slides, turns and flips from Rotations and the enlargements from Dilations are all transformations.

head: Rule $T(x, y)$
What it does
Keeps every distance?
rows: dilation, scale factor 2, center the origin
blocks.cap: Some transformations written as functions of the coordinates.

blocks.html: A rigid motion is a transformation that keeps every distance the same: for any two points, $P'Q' = PQ$. Keeping distances keeps everything else too: side lengths, angle measures, area, straightness. To show a rule is not rigid, one pair of points whose distance changes is enough.

blocks.name: transform
blocks.cap: Try each transformation. Translations, reflections and rotations keep the triangle's size; a dilation changes it.

blocks.html: A transformation is a function on points: $T(P) = P'$. Rigid motions (translations, reflections, rotations) keep every distance and angle; dilations and stretches do not.

blocks.title: Applying a rule
blocks.q: $T(x, y) = (y, -x)$. Find the images of $A(1, 2)$, $B(4, 2)$ and $C(1, 5)$.
steps: Put each point into the rule: the new $x$ is the old $y$; the new $y$ is the opposite of the old $x$.
This rule turns the plane $90^\circ$ clockwise about the origin.

blocks.title: Is it rigid?
blocks.q: Is $T(x, y) = (2x, y)$ a rigid motion?
blocks.a: No. It stretches the plane sideways, so it is not rigid.

blocks.title: Working backward
steps: $T$ subtracts 4 from $x$ and adds 1 to $y$; undo both.

blocks.html: Thinking any transformation that keeps the shape is rigid. A dilation keeps the shape but changes the size, so it is not rigid. A stretch like $(x, 3y)$ changes both size and shape. Check by computing one length before and after: a rigid motion never changes it.

blocks.html: In Transformations as Functions you used coordinate rules. To prove things about rigid motions, we need definitions that do not depend on a grid, built from tools you already have: circles, perpendicular bisectors and parallel lines from Constructing Perpendicular and Parallel Lines.

items: Translation by a vector $\vec{v}$: every point moves the same distance in the same direction, so each segment $\overline{PP'}$ is parallel to $\vec{v}$ and has the same length.
Reflection over a line $\ell$: a point on $\ell$ stays put; any other point $P$ goes to the point $P'$ for which $\ell$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PP'}$.

Rotation about a center $C$ by an angle $\theta$: $C$ stays put; any other point $P$ goes to the point $P'$ with $CP' = CP$ (same circle around $C$) and $m\angle PCP' = \theta$, counterclockwise when $\theta$ is positive.

blocks.html: These definitions use only ideas we can construct and reason about. That is what lets us prove that rigid motions keep distances, and later that they explain congruence. For example, a reflection keeps $PQ$ because the two halves of the picture on either side of $\ell$ are mirror images made of congruent right triangles.

blocks.name: transform
blocks.cap: Pick a reflection line and watch: the line is always the perpendicular bisector of each segment joining a point to its image.

blocks.title: Reflecting over a vertical line
blocks.q: Reflect $P(5, 1)$ over the line $x = 2$.
steps: $P$ is $3$ units right of the line, so $P'$ is $3$ units left of it: $x = 2 - 3 = -1$.
The line is vertical, so $\overline{PP'}$ is horizontal and $y$ does not change.
$P' = (-1, 1)$. Check: the midpoint of $\overline{PP'}$ is $(2, 1)$, on the line, and $\overline{PP'}$ is perpendicular to it.

blocks.title: Rotating about a point that is not the origin
blocks.q: Rotate $P(3, 1)$ by $90^\circ$ counterclockwise about $C(1, 2)$.
steps: A $90^\circ$ counterclockwise turn sends $\langle a, b \rangle$ to $\langle -b, a \rangle$: $\langle 1, 2 \rangle$.
Add back $C$: $P' = (1 + 1, 2 + 2) = (2, 4)$ (shown as $Q$). Check: $CP = CP' = \sqrt{5}$ and the angle at $C$ is a right angle.

blocks.title: Finding the mirror
blocks.q: A reflection sends $P(1, 4)$ to $P'(5, 4)$. What is the line of reflection?
steps: The line is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PP'}$.
Midpoint: $(3, 4)$. $\overline{PP'}$ is horizontal, so the bisector is vertical.

blocks.html: Translation: every point moves by the same vector. Reflection: the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each $\overline{PP'}$. Rotation: each point stays on its circle around the center and turns through the same angle.

Rotating about the origin when the center is somewhere else. The rule $(x, y) \to (-y, x)$ only works for the origin. For another center, first find each point's position relative to the center, rotate that, then add the center back. Check: the center-to-point distance must not change.

blocks.html: A symmetry of a figure is a rigid motion that carries the figure onto itself, so afterward it looks exactly the same. With the precise rotations and reflections from Precise Definitions of Rigid Motions, we can find every symmetry of a polygon.

In a regular polygon with $n$ sides, the vertices sit equally spaced on a circle around the center. Turning by one "vertex step," $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$, moves every vertex onto the next one, so the polygon lands on itself. Any multiple of that step works too, and nothing in between does. Each line through the center and a vertex (or the midpoint of a side) is a mirror line, giving $n$ reflections in all.

head: Shape

blocks.cap: Symmetries of common polygons. Every figure also has the "do nothing" symmetry, a turn of $0^\circ$ or $360^\circ$.

blocks.html: A regular polygon with $n$ sides has $n$ lines of symmetry and is carried onto itself by rotations of $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$ and its multiples.

blocks.title: A regular pentagon
blocks.q: List every rotation between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ that carries a regular pentagon onto itself.

blocks.title: A rectangle
blocks.q: Describe all the symmetries of a $2$ by $5$ rectangle.
steps: Reflections: the line through the midpoints of the long sides and the line through the midpoints of the short sides. The diagonals are not mirror lines: folding along one does not match the corners.
Rotations: $180^\circ$ about the center swaps opposite corners. A $90^\circ$ turn would put a long side where a short side was, so it fails.
blocks.a: Two reflections and the $180^\circ$ rotation (plus doing nothing).

blocks.html: Counting only the full turn, or only "nice" angles like $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. A regular pentagon has no $90^\circ$ symmetry, but it does have $72^\circ$. Always divide $360^\circ$ by the number of sides, then list the multiples.

blocks.html: You can follow one transformation with another. The result, called a composition, is again a transformation: $P \to A(P) \to B(A(P))$. Composing the rigid motions from Precise Definitions of Rigid Motions always gives a rigid motion, since each step keeps distances.

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.q: $P = (2, 1)$. (a) Translate by $\langle 3, 0 \rangle$, then reflect over the $y$-axis. (b) Reflect first, then translate.
steps: The results differ, so these two transformations do not commute.

blocks.html: Two reflections make something new. Reflect over a line $\ell$, then over a parallel line $m$ a distance $d$ away: a point $x$ units from $\ell$ ends up shifted $2d$ in the direction from $\ell$ to $m$, whatever $x$ is, so the composition is a translation by $2d$. If the two mirror lines cross at $C$ with angle $\theta$ between them, the composition is a rotation about $C$ by $2\theta$. Every rigid motion can be built from at most three reflections.

blocks.name: transform
blocks.cap: Try a reflection, then reflect the image again by changing the line. Two parallel mirrors make a slide; crossing mirrors make a turn.

blocks.title: Two reflections over parallel lines
blocks.q: Reflect $P(0, 2)$ over $x = 1$, then over $x = 4$. What single transformation does the same thing?
steps: First: $P$ is 1 unit left of $x = 1$, so it goes to $(2, 2)$.
Second: $(2, 2)$ is 2 units left of $x = 4$, so it goes to $(6, 2)$.
The lines are $3$ units apart, and $P$ moved $6 = 2 \cdot 3$ units right.

blocks.title: Finding a sequence
blocks.q: $\triangle ABC$ has $A(1, 1)$, $B(3, 1)$, $C(1, 2)$. $\triangle DEF$ has $D(-1, -3)$, $E(-3, -3)$, $F(-1, -4)$. Find rigid motions that map $\triangle ABC$ onto $\triangle DEF$ in order.
steps: Compare shapes: $AB$ points right, but $DE$ points left; $AC$ points up, but $DF$ points down. A $180^\circ$ rotation about the origin flips both: $(x, y) \to (-x, -y)$.
Each image is 2 units above its target, so translate by $\langle 0, -2 \rangle$.
blocks.a: Rotate $180^\circ$ about the origin, then translate by $\langle 0, -2 \rangle$.

blocks.html: A composition does one transformation, then the next. The order can change the result. Two reflections in parallel lines make a translation (twice the gap); in crossing lines, a rotation (twice the angle).

Assuming the order never matters. Sometimes it does not (two translations, or two rotations about the same center), but often it does, as in the first example. Check by sending one point through both orders.

blocks.html: "Same size and shape" is a good first idea, but it is hard to check or prove. Geometry makes it precise with the rigid motions from Composing Transformations: two figures are congruent if some sequence of translations, reflections and rotations carries one exactly onto the other.

Rigid motions keep every distance and every angle. So if a rigid motion carries figure $F$ onto figure $G$, each part of $F$ lands on a part of $G$ with the same length or measure. Congruent figures therefore have all corresponding parts equal. The definition also works for any shape, not just polygons: two circles, two curves, two letters of the alphabet.

blocks.name: transform
blocks.cap: Find a rigid motion that moves the triangle onto the dashed outline. Any rule that lands exactly on it shows the two triangles are congruent.

blocks.html: Two figures are congruent ($\cong$) when a sequence of rigid motions maps one onto the other. Then every pair of matching sides and angles is equal.

blocks.title: Finding the motion
blocks.q: $\triangle ABC$ has $A(1, 2)$, $B(5, 2)$, $C(1, 4)$ and $\triangle DEF$ has $D(-2, -1)$, $E(-2, -5)$, $F(0, -1)$, with $A \to D$, $B \to E$, $C \to F$. Show the triangles are congruent.
steps: $\overline{AB}$ points right (4 units); $\overline{DE}$ points down (4 units). $\overline{AC}$ points up (2 units); $\overline{DF}$ points right (2 units). Right turns into down and up turns into right: that is a $90^\circ$ clockwise turn, $(x, y) \to (y, -x)$.
Each image is 4 units right of its target, so translate by $\langle -4, 0 \rangle$: $(2, -1) \to (-2, -1) = D$, $(2, -5) \to (-2, -5) = E$ and $(4, -1) \to (0, -1) = F$.
blocks.a: A $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation about the origin followed by a translation of $\langle -4, 0 \rangle$ maps $\triangle ABC$ onto $\triangle DEF$, so they are congruent.

blocks.title: Showing two figures are not congruent
blocks.q: $\triangle PQR$ has sides $5$, $5$ and $6$. $\triangle STU$ has sides $5$, $6$ and $6$. Can they be congruent?
steps: A rigid motion keeps every length, so congruent triangles have the same three side lengths.
blocks.a: No rigid motion can map one onto the other: they are not congruent.

blocks.html: Deciding congruence from one number, like equal areas or equal perimeters. A $2 \times 6$ rectangle and a $3 \times 4$ rectangle both have area 12, but no rigid motion maps one onto the other. Check matching lengths and angles, or find the motion.

blocks.html: When a rigid motion carries $\triangle ABC$ onto $\triangle DEF$ (see Congruence and Rigid Motions), it sends each vertex to a specific vertex. The congruence statement $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$ records exactly that: $A \to D$, $B \to E$, $C \to F$.

The order of the letters is the correspondence. Matching letters in the same position gives the six pairs of corresponding parts, and each pair is equal because the rigid motion keeps lengths and angles. The picture can be turned or flipped any way; the letters still tell the truth.

blocks.title: Listing the parts
blocks.q: $\triangle PQR \cong \triangle XZY$. Which side corresponds to $\overline{QR}$, and which angle is congruent to $\angle R$?
steps: Pair the letters by position: $P \leftrightarrow X$, $Q \leftrightarrow Z$, $R \leftrightarrow Y$.

blocks.title: Using the parts
blocks.q: $\triangle KLM \cong \triangle RST$, $m\angle K = 48^\circ$, $m\angle L = 75^\circ$ and $ST = 3x - 4$ while $LM = 11$. Find $m\angle T$ and $x$.
steps: $\angle T$ matches $\angle M$. In $\triangle KLM$, $m\angle M = 180 - 48 - 75 = 57^\circ$, so $m\angle T = 57^\circ$.

blocks.html: When you write a congruence statement yourself, list the first triangle's vertices in any order, then list the second triangle's vertices in the matching order. $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$ and $\triangle BCA \cong \triangle EFD$ say the same thing; $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle EDF$ says something different.

Matching parts by where they sit on the page. If the second triangle is turned or flipped, its "bottom side" may not match the first triangle's bottom side. Always pair letters by their position in the congruence statement. Check: a statement like $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle BCA$ written for two triangles in the same spot is a warning sign; rewrite it carefully.

blocks.html: Do you need all six pairs of corresponding parts from Corresponding Parts to know two triangles are congruent? No. Three well-chosen pairs force the rest. The trick is choosing the right three, and the proof uses the rigid motions you already know. You will use these criteria in proofs, so the writing skills from Writing a Proof matter here.

head: Criterion
What must match
Why it works (sketch)
rows: the third vertex is where two circles cross; the motion has nowhere else to put it
two sides and the angle between them
the angle fixes the direction of the second side, and its length fixes where it ends
two angles and the side between them
the two angles fix two rays from the ends of the side, and two rays meet in one point
blocks.cap: The three basic congruence criteria.

blocks.html: Here is why SAS works. Suppose $AB = DE$, $AC = DF$ and $\angle A \cong \angle D$. Translate so $A$ lands on $D$. Rotate about $D$ so ray $AB$ lies along ray $DE$; since $AB = DE$, $B$ lands on $E$. If $C$ ends up on the other side of $\overline{DE}$ from $F$, reflect over $\overleftrightarrow{DE}$. Now the angles at $D$ match, so ray $AC$ lies along ray $DF$, and $AC = DF$ puts $C$ on $F$. All three vertices match: the triangles are congruent.

blocks.cap: Why SSA fails: both triangles have the marked side, the marked angle at the left vertex, and the double-marked side, yet they are different. The angle is not between the two sides.

opts.label: Two different triangles with two congruent sides and a congruent angle that is not between them

blocks.title: Choosing the criterion
blocks.q: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$, $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{DE}$, $\angle B \cong \angle E$ and $\overline{BC} \cong \overline{EF}$. Are they congruent? By what?
steps: The marked angle, $\angle B$, is where the marked sides $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BC}$ meet: it is the included angle.
Two sides and the included angle: SAS.

blocks.title: What is missing?
blocks.q: $\angle A \cong \angle D$ and $\angle C \cong \angle F$. Which pair of sides would prove the triangles congruent by ASA?
steps: ASA needs the side between the two angles.

blocks.html: SSS, SAS and ASA each prove two triangles congruent. In SAS the angle must be between the two sides; in ASA the side must be between the two angles.

Accepting SSA or AAA. With SSA (an angle that is not between the two sides), two different triangles can fit, as the picture above shows. With AAA, a triangle and an enlarged copy have the same angles but different sides. Check where the angle sits relative to the sides before naming a criterion.

blocks.html: SSS, SAS and ASA gave you SSS, SAS and ASA. Two more criteria save time: AAS for any triangle, and HL for right triangles.

AAS: if two angles of one triangle match two angles of another, the third angles match too, because each set adds to $180^\circ$. So a side that is not between the two given angles is still between two matching angles, and ASA applies.
HL: in right triangles, if the hypotenuses match and one pair of legs matches, the Pythagorean theorem makes the other legs match: $\sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$ is the same for both. Then SSS applies.

blocks.cap: HL: right angles, congruent hypotenuses (one tick) and one pair of congruent legs (two ticks).

opts.label: Two right triangles with congruent hypotenuses and one pair of congruent legs

blocks.html: AAS: two angles and a side that is not between them. HL: right triangles with congruent hypotenuses and one pair of congruent legs. Both prove congruence.

blocks.title: AAS
blocks.q: $\angle A \cong \angle D$, $\angle B \cong \angle E$ and $\overline{BC} \cong \overline{EF}$. Which criterion applies?
steps: The side $\overline{BC}$ touches $\angle B$ but not $\angle A$: it is not between the two angles, so this is not ASA.
Two angles and a non-included side: AAS.

blocks.title: HL with numbers
blocks.q: Right triangles $PQR$ and $STU$ have right angles at $R$ and $U$. $PQ = ST = 13$ and $PR = SU = 5$. Show they are congruent and find $TU$.
steps: $\overline{PQ}$ and $\overline{ST}$ are opposite the right angles: they are the hypotenuses, and they are congruent.
$\overline{PR}$ and $\overline{SU}$ are matching legs, also congruent. So $\triangle PQR \cong \triangle STU$ by HL.

blocks.title: Choosing among five
blocks.q: Two triangles have $\angle A \cong \angle D$, $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{DE}$, $\angle B \cong \angle E$. Is this AAS or ASA?
steps: The side $\overline{AB}$ joins the two marked angles, $A$ and $B$.
blocks.a: ASA (the side is between the angles).

blocks.html: Using HL for triangles that are not right triangles. Hypotenuse-leg is really SSA, which fails in general; it only works because the right angle makes the Pythagorean theorem available. Check for a right angle (given or marked) before writing HL.

blocks.html: Most proofs about triangles follow one pattern: find three pairs of congruent parts, prove the triangles congruent with one of the criteria from AAS and Hypotenuse-Leg and SSS, SAS and ASA, then use the fact that corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent (CPCTC) to get the part you really want.

items: A shared side: $\overline{BD} \cong \overline{BD}$ by the Reflexive Property.
Vertical angles where two segments cross: congruent by the Vertical Angles Theorem.
Parallel lines: alternate interior angles are congruent.
Midpoints and bisectors: they give two congruent segments or angles, by definition.
Perpendicular lines: they give right angles, and all right angles are congruent. cap: Hidden congruent parts to look for.

blocks.html: CPCTC is not a new idea: once a rigid motion carries one triangle onto the other (that is what congruent means), every part lands on its partner. The criteria let us know such a motion exists without finding it.

blocks.title: A kite (SSS, then CPCTC)
blocks.q: Given: $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CB}$ and $\overline{AD} \cong \overline{CD}$. Prove: $\angle A \cong \angle C$.
blocks.a: Proved: the triangles are congruent first, then their matching angles.

blocks.title: Crossing segments (SAS)
blocks.q: Given: $E$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AD}$ and of $\overline{BC}$. Prove: $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{DC}$.
steps: 1. $E$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{BC}$ — Given.
4. $\triangle ABE \cong \triangle DCE$ — SAS (the vertical angles are between the pairs of sides).

blocks.html: Plan backward from the goal: which two triangles contain the parts you want? Find three pairs of congruent parts (look for shared sides, vertical angles, parallel lines, midpoints), name the criterion, and finish with CPCTC.

Using CPCTC before the triangles are proved congruent. CPCTC is only a valid reason on a line after the congruence statement. If a proof says "$\overline{AB} \cong \overline{DC}$ by CPCTC" in step 2, it is using what it has not yet shown. Check: every CPCTC line should point back to an earlier "$\triangle \ldots \cong \triangle \ldots$" line.

blocks.html: In Triangle Angle Sum and Exterior Angles you tore the corners off a paper triangle and saw that they make a straight line. That convinced you; now we prove it for every triangle at once, using the parallel-line theorems from Proving Theorems about Lines and Angles.

Triangle Sum Theorem. Take any $\triangle ABC$. Through $B$, draw the line parallel to $\overline{AC}$ (there is exactly one). At $B$ three angles now sit side by side on that line: angle 1, then $\angle ABC$, then angle 3. Angle 1 and $\angle A$ are alternate interior angles, so they are congruent; so are angle 3 and $\angle C$. The three angles at $B$ make a straight angle, $180^\circ$, so $m\angle A + m\angle ABC + m\angle C = 180^\circ$.

blocks.html: Exterior Angle Theorem. Extend one side of a triangle. The angle outside, the exterior angle, forms a linear pair with the interior angle next to it. Both that pair and the three interior angles add to $180^\circ$, so the exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles (the two not touching it).
The interior angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

blocks.cap: Drag the corners: the three angles always add to $180^\circ$. "Tear off the corners" lines them up on a straight line.

blocks.q: In $\triangle PQR$, $m\angle P = 47^\circ$ and $m\angle Q = 68^\circ$. Find $m\angle R$.

blocks.title: An exterior angle with algebra
blocks.q: Side $\overline{BC}$ of $\triangle ABC$ is extended to $D$. $m\angle ACD = (5x - 4)^\circ$, $m\angle A = (2x + 10)^\circ$ and $m\angle B = 40^\circ$. Find $m\angle ACD$.
steps: Exterior angle = sum of the remote interior angles: $5x - 4 = (2x + 10) + 40$.

blocks.html: Setting the exterior angle equal to the interior angle next to it, or to all three interior angles. The angle next to it is its supplement, and all three interior angles add to $180^\circ$. The exterior angle equals only the two remote angles. Check: exterior + adjacent interior $= 180^\circ$.

blocks.html: An isosceles triangle has at least two congruent sides, called the legs. The angle between the legs is the vertex angle; the third side is the base, and the two angles at its ends are the base angles. With the congruence proofs from Proofs with Congruent Triangles we can prove what those base angles do.

Isosceles Triangle Theorem. In $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = AC$, draw the bisector of $\angle A$, meeting $\overline{BC}$ at $D$. Then $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}$ (given), $\angle BAD \cong \angle CAD$ (bisector) and $\overline{AD} \cong \overline{AD}$ (shared). So $\triangle ABD \cong \triangle ACD$ by SAS, and by CPCTC $\angle B \cong \angle C$. The converse also holds: if two angles of a triangle are congruent, the sides opposite them are congruent (the same picture with AAS).

blocks.html: The angles opposite the congruent sides (the base angles) are congruent, and if two angles are congruent, so are the sides opposite them. An equilateral triangle is equiangular: each angle is $60^\circ$.

blocks.title: From the vertex angle
blocks.q: In isosceles $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = AC$, the vertex angle measures $40^\circ$. Find the base angles.
steps: The base angles are equal and share $180 - 40 = 140^\circ$.

blocks.title: With algebra
blocks.q: In $\triangle PQR$, $PQ = PR$, $m\angle Q = (3x + 4)^\circ$ and $m\angle R = (5x - 20)^\circ$. Find $m\angle P$.
steps: $\angle Q$ and $\angle R$ are opposite the equal sides, so $3x + 4 = 5x - 20$, and $x = 12$.
Each base angle is $3(12) + 4 = 40^\circ$, so $m\angle P = 180 - 80 = 100^\circ$.

blocks.title: The converse
blocks.q: In $\triangle XYZ$, $m\angle X = m\angle Y = 52^\circ$, $XZ = 2n + 3$ and $YZ = 4n - 9$. Find $XZ$.
steps: Equal angles $X$ and $Y$ mean the sides opposite them are equal: $\overline{YZ}$ (opposite $X$) and $\overline{XZ}$ (opposite $Y$).

blocks.html: Marking the wrong pair of angles as base angles, especially when the triangle is turned. The base angles are opposite the congruent sides, not next to them; the vertex angle is where the two congruent sides meet. Check: each base angle touches the base and one leg.

blocks.html: In Constructing Perpendicular and Parallel Lines you constructed perpendicular bisectors and said they hold the points that are equally far from both endpoints. Now we prove it with Proofs with Congruent Triangles, and use it to find the one point that is equally far from all three vertices of a triangle.

Perpendicular Bisector Theorem: if $P$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$, then $PA = PB$. If $M$ is the midpoint, the triangles $PMA$ and $PMB$ share $\overline{PM}$, have right angles at $M$ and $MA = MB$, so they are congruent by SAS and $PA = PB$. Converse: if $PA = PB$, then $P$ is on the perpendicular bisector (the two right triangles are congruent by SSS, so the angles at $M$ are equal and therefore right).

The circumcenter. Let $O$ be where the perpendicular bisectors of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BC}$ cross. Then $OA = OB$ and $OB = OC$, so $OA = OC$, which puts $O$ on the third bisector too. All three bisectors meet at $O$, and the circle centered at $O$ through $A$ passes through all three vertices: the circumscribed circle.

blocks.name: geo-fig
blocks.cap: The three perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcenter $O$. The red radii $OA$, $OB$ and $OC$ are equal.

opts.label: A triangle with its three perpendicular bisectors meeting at the circumcenter O, and the circle through all three vertices

blocks.html: A point is on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$ exactly when it is equally far from $A$ and $B$. The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle meet at the circumcenter, the center of the circle through all three vertices.

blocks.title: A point on a bisector
blocks.q: $P$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$, $PA = 4x - 3$ and $PB = 2x + 9$. Find $PA$.

blocks.title: The circumcenter on a grid
blocks.q: Find the circumcenter of $A(0, 0)$, $B(6, 0)$ and $C(2, 4)$.
steps: $\overline{AB}$ is horizontal with midpoint $(3, 0)$, so its perpendicular bisector is $x = 3$.
The circumcenter is $(3, y)$ with $OA = OC$: $3^2 + y^2 = (3 - 2)^2 + (y - 4)^2$.

blocks.html: Where the circumcenter lands depends on the largest angle: inside an acute triangle, at the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.
Thinking the circumcenter is equally far from the sides. It is equally far from the three vertices. (The point equally far from the sides is the incenter, in Incenter, Centroid and Orthocenter.)

blocks.html: The perpendicular bisectors of a triangle meet at one point, the circumcenter of Perpendicular Bisectors and the Circumcenter. Three other families of segments also meet at single points, and each point has its own job.

head: Segments

blocks.html: Mixing up medians and altitudes, or expecting every center to be inside. A median ends at a midpoint; an altitude ends at a right angle. They coincide only in special cases. blocks.html: A midsegment of a triangle joins the midpoints of two sides. Every triangle has three. With the midpoint formula from Distance and Midpoint Formulas and the parallel-line facts behind Triangle Sum and Exterior Angle Proofs, we can show that a midsegment always does two surprising things.

Put the triangle on a grid in a smart spot: $A(0, 0)$, $B(2a, 0)$ and $C(2b, 2c)$. (Using $2a$, $2b$, $2c$ keeps the midpoints free of fractions.) The midpoint of $\overline{AC}$ is $D(b, c)$ and the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ is $E(a + b, c)$. $\overline{DE}$ is horizontal, just like $\overline{AB}$, so they are parallel. $DE = (a + b) - b = a$, while $AB = 2a$. Since the triangle was any triangle, this holds for all of them.

blocks.html: You proved in Triangle Sum and Exterior Angle Proofs that a triangle's angles add to $180^\circ$. Every polygon can be cut into triangles, so the same fact gives the angle sum of any polygon.

Interior angles. In a convex polygon with $n$ sides, draw every diagonal from one vertex. They cut it into $n - 2$ triangles (each side except the two at that vertex gets its own triangle), and the triangles' angles together make up exactly the polygon's angles. So the sum is $(n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ$.
Exterior angles. At each vertex, the interior and exterior angles form a linear pair, so all $n$ pairs total $n \cdot 180^\circ$. Subtract the interior sum: $n \cdot 180^\circ - (n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ = 360^\circ$. It is one full turn, the amount you turn while walking once around the polygon.

blocks.html: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel; that is the definition. Everything else about it can be proved with the congruent-triangle methods of Proofs with Congruent Triangles and the angle sums of Polygon Angle Sums.

Draw diagonal $\overline{AC}$ in parallelogram $ABCD$. Because $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{DC}$, the alternate interior angles $\angle BAC$ and $\angle DCA$ are congruent; because $\overline{AD} \parallel \overline{BC}$, so are $\angle DAC$ and $\angle BCA$. With the shared side $\overline{AC}$, $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ by ASA. CPCTC then gives $AB = CD$, $BC = DA$ and $\angle B \cong \angle D$. Using the other diagonal the same way gives $\angle A \cong \angle C$. Finally, the triangles $AEB$ and $CED$ formed where the diagonals cross are congruent by ASA, so $AE = EC$ and $BE = ED$.

blocks.q: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram with $AB = 3x + 4$ and $CD = 5x - 10$. Find $AB$.

$m\angle A = 86^\circ$ and $m\angle B = 94^\circ$. Opposite angles match: $m\angle C = 86^\circ$, $m\angle D = 94^\circ$.

blocks.html: Assuming the diagonals of every parallelogram are congruent or perpendicular. They always bisect each other, but in a long, slanted parallelogram one diagonal is much longer than the other, and they cross at an angle that is not $90^\circ$. Congruent diagonals happen only in rectangles, perpendicular ones only in rhombuses.

blocks.html: Properties of Parallelograms went from "parallelogram" to its properties. Now we go the other way: which properties are enough to prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram? Each test below is a converse of a property, and each one is a theorem.

items: Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel (the definition).
Both pairs of opposite sides are congruent.
Both pairs of opposite angles are congruent.
The diagonals bisect each other.
One pair of opposite sides is both parallel and congruent.

blocks.html: Here is the proof of the second test. Suppose $AB = CD$ and $BC = DA$. Draw diagonal $\overline{AC}$. Then $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ by SSS, so $\angle BAC \cong \angle DCA$ by CPCTC. Those are alternate interior angles for $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{DC}$ with transversal $\overline{AC}$, so by the converse of the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{DC}$. The same argument with the other pair of angles gives $\overline{AD} \parallel \overline{BC}$.

A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if both pairs of opposite sides are congruent, or both pairs of opposite angles are congruent, or its diagonals bisect each other, or one pair of opposite sides is both parallel and congruent.

blocks.title: Solving so it works
blocks.q: The diagonals of $ABCD$ meet at $E$, with $AE = 3x - 2$, $EC = x + 6$, $BE = y + 5$ and $ED = 2y - 1$. Find $x$ and $y$ so that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
steps: If the diagonals bisect each other, it is a parallelogram. So set $AE = EC$ and $BE = ED$.

blocks.title: A proof with coordinates
blocks.q: Is $A(-1, 1)$, $B(4, 2)$, $C(6, 6)$, $D(1, 5)$ a parallelogram?
steps: Test the diagonals: midpoint of $\overline{AC}$ is $\left(\frac{-1 + 6}{2}, \frac{1 + 6}{2}\right) = \left(\frac{5}{2}, \frac{7}{2}\right)$.
Same point, so the diagonals bisect each other.

blocks.title: Not enough
blocks.q: A quadrilateral has one pair of parallel sides and the other pair congruent. Must it be a parallelogram?
steps: An isosceles trapezoid fits: its bases are parallel and its legs are congruent.
But its legs are not parallel, so it is not a parallelogram.
blocks.a: No. The parallel pair and the congruent pair must be the same pair.

blocks.html: Three kinds of parallelograms get their own names. A rectangle has four right angles. A rhombus has four congruent sides. A square is both. Each one has every property from Properties of Parallelograms, plus more, and those extra properties give new tests like the ones in Proving a Quadrilateral Is a Parallelogram.

Rectangle diagonals are congruent. In rectangle $ABCD$, $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DCB$ share $\overline{BC}$, have $AB = DC$, and have right angles at $B$ and $C$. By SAS they are congruent, so $AC = DB$.
Rhombus diagonals are perpendicular. In rhombus $ABCD$ with diagonals meeting at $E$, $\triangle AEB \cong \triangle CEB$ by SSS ($AB = CB$, $AE = CE$, shared $\overline{BE}$). So the angles at $E$ are congruent, and since they form a linear pair, each is $90^\circ$. The same triangles show that each diagonal bisects the angles it passes through.

blocks.html: A coordinate grid turns geometry facts into algebra you can check. You have three tools: slope for parallel and perpendicular lines (from Parallel and Perpendicular Lines), the distance formula for lengths, and the midpoint formula. Together they can prove the facts from Rectangles, Rhombuses and Squares.

items: Parallel sides: equal slopes. Perpendicular sides: slopes whose product is $-1$ (or one horizontal and one vertical).
Congruent sides or diagonals: equal distances.
Diagonals that bisect each other: the same midpoint.

blocks.html: A proof with specific numbers shows one example. To prove a fact about every rectangle, place a general rectangle on the grid using letters: $(0, 0)$, $(a, 0)$, $(a, b)$, $(0, b)$. Any rectangle can be moved by a rigid motion to sit this way, and rigid motions keep lengths and angles, so the algebra covers them all. Putting a corner at the origin and sides on the axes makes most coordinates zero and the algebra short.

blocks.title: Classify a quadrilateral
blocks.q: Classify $A(0, 0)$, $B(4, 3)$, $C(4, 8)$, $D(0, 5)$.
steps: Slopes: $AB$: $\frac{3}{4}$; $BC$: undefined (vertical); $CD$: $\frac{8 - 5}{4 - 0} = \frac{3}{4}$; $DA$: undefined. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel: a parallelogram.
Lengths: $AB = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5$ and $BC = 5$. All four sides are 5: a rhombus.
Right angle? $\overline{AB}$ (slope $\frac{3}{4}$) and $\overline{BC}$ (vertical) are not perpendicular.
blocks.a: A rhombus that is not a square.

blocks.title: A general proof
blocks.q: Prove that the diagonals of any parallelogram bisect each other.
steps: Place it as $A(0, 0)$, $B(a, 0)$, $C(a + b, c)$, $D(b, c)$. Then $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{DC}$ are both horizontal with length $a$, so opposite sides are parallel by design.
Midpoint of $\overline{AC}$: $\left(\frac{a + b}{2}, \frac{c}{2}\right)$. Midpoint of $\overline{BD}$: $\left(\frac{a + b}{2}, \frac{c}{2}\right)$.
The midpoints are the same point, so each diagonal cuts the other in half.
blocks.a: Proved for every parallelogram, because the letters stand for any values.

blocks.title: Rectangle diagonals
blocks.q: Prove that the diagonals of a rectangle are congruent.
steps: Place the rectangle at $(0, 0)$, $(a, 0)$, $(a, b)$, $(0, b)$.
One diagonal: from $(0, 0)$ to $(a, b)$, length $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. The other: from $(a, 0)$ to $(0, b)$, length $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
blocks.a: The lengths are equal, so the diagonals are congruent.

blocks.html: A dilation with center $O$ and scale factor $k > 0$ sends each point $P$ to the point $P'$ on ray $\overrightarrow{OP}$ with $OP' = k \cdot OP$. The center stays put. In Transformations as Functions you saw that a dilation is not a rigid motion; here we pin down exactly what it does change and what it keeps.

Put the center at the origin. Then the dilation is $(x, y) \to (kx, ky)$. For two points $P(x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2)$, the slope of $\overline{P'Q'}$ is $\frac{k y_2 - k y_1}{k x_2 - k x_1} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$: the same slope, so the image is parallel to the original (or on the same line, if that line passes through the center). The length is $\sqrt{k^2 (x_2 - x_1)^2 + k^2 (y_2 - y_1)^2} = k \cdot PQ$. And since every side keeps its direction, every angle keeps its measure.

blocks.cap: Change $k$ and the center. Each side of the image stays parallel to the original side, its length is multiplied by $k$, and the angles never change.

blocks.html: A dilation by $k$ multiplies every length by $k$, keeps every angle, and sends each line to a parallel line (a line through the center goes to itself). $k > 1$ enlarges; $0 < k < 1$ shrinks.

steps: $k = \frac{A'B'}{AB} = \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}$. It is less than 1, so the triangle shrinks.

blocks.title: What happens to angles

blocks.html: Two figures are similar ($\sim$) if a sequence of rigid motions and dilations carries one onto the other. This builds on Congruence and Rigid Motions (rigid motions only) by also allowing a change of size, using the dilations of Properties of Dilations.

Rigid motions keep lengths and angles. A dilation keeps angles and multiplies every length by the same $k$. So a similarity transformation keeps every angle and multiplies every length by one scale factor. For similar triangles $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ that means: corresponding angles are congruent, and $\frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{EF}{BC} = \frac{FD}{CA} = k$.

blocks.cap: A dilation followed by a rigid motion produces a similar figure: same angles, proportional sides.

blocks.html: Similar figures have congruent corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. The ratio of corresponding lengths is the scale factor, and it applies to every length, including perimeters.

blocks.title: Finding a missing side
blocks.q: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ with $AB = 6$, $BC = 9$ and $DE = 10$. Find $EF$.
steps: The scale factor from $ABC$ to $DEF$ is $\frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{10}{6} = \frac{5}{3}$.

blocks.title: Describing the transformation
blocks.q: $\triangle ABC$ has $A(1, 1)$, $B(3, 1)$, $C(1, 2)$. $\triangle DEF$ has $D(-1, 4)$, $E(5, 4)$, $F(-1, 7)$. Describe a similarity transformation from $ABC$ to $DEF$.
steps: Compare sides: $AB = 2$ and $DE = 6$; $AC = 1$ and $DF = 3$. Scale factor 3, and the shapes face the same way.
Each image is 4 left and 1 up from its target... check: $(3, 3) \to (-1, 4)$ is $\langle -4, 1 \rangle$. Translate by $\langle -4, 1 \rangle$: $B \to (5, 4)$, $C \to (-1, 7)$.
blocks.a: Dilate by 3 about the origin, then translate by $\langle -4, 1 \rangle$.

blocks.title: Are all rectangles similar?
blocks.q: Are a $2 \times 3$ rectangle and a $4 \times 9$ rectangle similar?
steps: All angles are $90^\circ$, so only the sides matter. Short sides: $\frac{4}{2} = 2$. Long sides: $\frac{9}{3} = 3$.
The ratios differ, so no single scale factor works.

blocks.html: Matching sides out of order. In $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$, side $\overline{AB}$ matches $\overline{DE}$ because of the letter order, just as with congruence. If you compare $AB$ with $EF$, you get a wrong scale factor. Check: in a scale factor larger than 1, every side of the bigger figure should be paired with a smaller side of the other.

blocks.html: Checking all six parts is a lot of work. For triangles, two pairs of congruent angles are enough. The proof uses the definition of similarity from Similarity Through Transformations and the angle sum from Triangle Sum and Exterior Angle Proofs.

Suppose $\angle A \cong \angle D$ and $\angle B \cong \angle E$. Dilate $\triangle ABC$ by $k = \frac{DE}{AB}$. Its image $\triangle A'B'C'$ has $A'B' = DE$, and the dilation keeps angles, so $\angle A' \cong \angle D$ and $\angle B' \cong \angle E$. Now $\triangle A'B'C' \cong \triangle DEF$ by ASA, so a rigid motion carries it onto $\triangle DEF$. The dilation followed by that rigid motion is a similarity transformation: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$.
AA Similarity: if two angles of one triangle are congruent to two angles of another, the triangles are similar. (The third angles then match automatically.)

blocks.title: A line parallel to one side
blocks.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$ with $D$ on $\overline{AB}$ and $E$ on $\overline{AC}$. $AD = 4$, $DB = 6$ and $DE = 5$. Find $BC$.
steps: $\angle A$ is shared, and $\angle ADE \cong \angle ABC$ (corresponding angles). So $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ by AA.
Match whole side to whole side: $AB = 4 + 6 = 10$, so the scale factor from $ADE$ to $ABC$ is $\frac{10}{4} = \frac{5}{2}$.

blocks.title: Shadows
blocks.q: A $6$ ft person casts a $4$ ft shadow at the same moment a tree casts a $30$ ft shadow. How tall is the tree?
steps: The sun's rays hit both at the same angle, and both stand straight up, so the two right triangles are similar by AA.

blocks.title: An hourglass
blocks.q: $\overline{AE}$ and $\overline{BD}$ cross at $C$, with $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{DE}$. $AC = 6$, $CE = 9$ and $AB = 8$. Find $DE$.
steps: $\angle ACB \cong \angle ECD$ (vertical angles) and $\angle A \cong \angle E$ (alternate interior angles). So $\triangle ACB \sim \triangle ECD$ by AA.
Scale factor from the small triangle to the large: $\frac{CE}{AC} = \frac{9}{6} = \frac{3}{2}$.

blocks.html: Using a part of a side where the whole side belongs. In the first example, $\frac{BC}{DE}$ must equal $\frac{AB}{AD}$ (whole side over whole side), not $\frac{DB}{AD}$. Check: write the triangles' names in matching order, $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$, and read the sides from them.

blocks.html: Proving AA Similarity uses angles only. Two more tests use side ratios, matching the congruence criteria SSS and SAS, but with "proportional" in place of "congruent."

items: SSS Similarity: all three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
SAS Similarity: two pairs of sides are in the same ratio, and the angles between them are congruent.

blocks.html: The proofs copy the AA proof. Dilate the first triangle by the common ratio $k$. Its sides now equal the second triangle's sides (SSS case), or two sides and the included angle match (SAS case). So the dilated triangle is congruent to the second one by SSS or SAS, and a dilation followed by a rigid motion is a similarity.

To compare sides, put each triangle's sides in order from shortest to longest and divide matching sides. If all the ratios are equal (SSS), or two are equal with a congruent included angle (SAS), the triangles are similar.

blocks.html: When a line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides, it creates a small triangle similar to the big one, as you saw in Proving AA Similarity and SSS and SAS Similarity. That similarity says something neat about the pieces of the sides.

In $\triangle ABC$ with $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$, $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ by AA, so $\frac{AB}{AD} = \frac{AC}{AE}$. Write $AB = AD + DB$ and $AC = AE + EC$: $\frac{AD + DB}{AD} = \frac{AE + EC}{AE}$, which is $1 + \frac{DB}{AD} = 1 + \frac{EC}{AE}$. Subtract 1 and flip both sides: $\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$. The converse is true too: if the sides are cut in the same ratio, the segment is parallel to the third side.

blocks.html: Triangle Proportionality Theorem: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally, $\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$. Conversely, a segment that divides two sides proportionally is parallel to the third side.

blocks.title: Parts and parts
blocks.q: $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$, $AD = 6$, $DB = 4$ and $AE = 9$. Find $EC$.

blocks.title: With algebra
blocks.q: $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$, $AD = x$, $DB = x + 3$, $AE = 10$ and $EC = 16$. Find $x$.

blocks.title: Is it parallel?
blocks.q: $D$ is on $\overline{AB}$ and $E$ is on $\overline{AC}$ with $AD = 5$, $DB = 7$, $AE = 8$ and $EC = 11$. Is $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$?
steps: They are not equal, so the sides are not cut proportionally.
blocks.a: No (though it is close to parallel).

blocks.html: A useful corollary. If three or more parallel lines cut two transversals, they cut them proportionally. Join the transversals with a segment and apply the theorem in each of the two triangles it makes. So if the parallel lines cut one transversal into pieces $4$ and $6$, and the matching first piece on the other transversal is $10$, the second is $\frac{6}{4} \cdot 10 = 15$.

Mixing a part on one side with a whole on the other, like $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$. Use parts with parts ($\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$) or wholes with wholes ($\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{AE}{AC}$). Check by labeling every segment in your proportion on the picture.

blocks.html: The midpoint from Distance and Midpoint Formulas splits a segment in the ratio $1 : 1$. Sometimes you need a point that splits it in another ratio, like $2 : 3$. The side-splitting idea from The Triangle Proportionality Theorem shows how.

Draw the right triangle under $\overline{AB}$, with legs along the grid. A point $P$ on $\overline{AB}$ with $AP : PB = a : b$ cuts the hypotenuse into $a + b$ equal parts and keeps $a$ of them. Lines through $P$ parallel to the legs cut the legs in the same ratio (the triangles are similar), so $P$ is $\frac{a}{a + b}$ of the way along in $x$ and in $y$. Its coordinates $(x, y)$ are $$x = x_1 + \tfrac{a}{a + b}(x_2 - x_1)$$ $$y = y_1 + \tfrac{a}{a + b}(y_2 - y_1)$$

blocks.html: Going $\frac{a}{b}$ of the way instead of $\frac{a}{a + b}$. With $AP : PB = 2 : 3$, the point is $\frac{2}{5}$ of the way, not $\frac{2}{3}$: the ratio compares the two pieces with each other, but you need a piece compared with the whole. blocks.html: Draw the altitude from the right angle of a right triangle to its hypotenuse. It splits the triangle into two smaller right triangles, and all three triangles are similar. You can prove it with Proving AA Similarity, and it leads to a new proof of the theorem from The Pythagorean Theorem.

In right $\triangle ABC$ (right angle at $C$) with altitude $\overline{CD}$, call the angle at $A$ $\alpha$ and the angle at $B$ $\beta$, so $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$. $\triangle ACD$ has a right angle at $D$ and the angle $\alpha$ at $A$, so its angle at $C$ is $\beta$. $\triangle CBD$ has a right angle at $D$ and $\beta$ at $B$, so its angle at $C$ is $\alpha$. All three triangles have angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $90^\circ$: they are similar by AA, with $\triangle ACD \sim \triangle CBD \sim \triangle ABC$.

blocks.cap: Left: the altitude $\overline{CD}$. Right: the three triangles turned the same way. Same angles, three sizes.

blocks.html: The altitude to the hypotenuse makes three similar right triangles. So the altitude is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse's two pieces, $CD^2 = AD \cdot DB$, and each leg is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse and the piece next to it: $AC^2 = AD \cdot AB$ and $BC^2 = DB \cdot AB$.

blocks.title: The altitude
blocks.q: The altitude to the hypotenuse splits it into $AD = 4$ and $DB = 9$. Find $CD$.

blocks.title: A leg
blocks.q: With $AD = 4$ and $DB = 9$ again, find $AC$.
steps: From $\triangle ACD \sim \triangle ABC$: $\frac{AD}{AC} = \frac{AC}{AB}$, so $AC^2 = AD \cdot AB$.
Check with the Pythagorean theorem in $\triangle ACD$: $4^2 + 6^2 = 52$.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: $CD = 12$ and $AD = 8$. Find $DB$.

blocks.html: The geometric mean of two positive numbers $p$ and $q$ is $\sqrt{pq}$: the number $x$ with $\frac{p}{x} = \frac{x}{q}$. The altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two pieces it creates.

Pairing a leg with the wrong piece of the hypotenuse. Leg $\overline{AC}$ touches $A$, so it goes with $AD$, the piece next to it: $AC^2 = AD \cdot AB$. Check: each leg's partner piece shares an endpoint with it.

blocks.html: You have used $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ since The Pythagorean Theorem, and seen why it works by rearranging areas. The similar triangles from Similar Right Triangles and the Geometric Mean give a short proof that uses no areas at all.

Let right $\triangle ABC$ have legs $a = BC$ and $b = AC$ and hypotenuse $c = AB$. The altitude from $C$ cuts the hypotenuse into $p = AD$ and $q = DB$, with $p + q = c$. From $\triangle ACD \sim \triangle ABC$: $\frac{p}{b} = \frac{b}{c}$, so $b^2 = cp$. From $\triangle CBD \sim \triangle ABC$: $\frac{q}{a} = \frac{a}{c}$, so $a^2 = cq$. Add: $a^2 + b^2 = cq + cp = c(p + q) = c \cdot c = c^2$.

blocks.title: The proof in two columns
blocks.q: Given: right $\triangle ABC$ with right angle at $C$ and altitude $\overline{CD}$. Prove: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
steps: 1. $\triangle ACD \sim \triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CBD \sim \triangle ABC$ — AA (each shares an acute angle with $\triangle ABC$, and all have a right angle).
2. $\frac{p}{b} = \frac{b}{c}$ and $\frac{q}{a} = \frac{a}{c}$ — Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional.
3. $b^2 = cp$ and $a^2 = cq$ — Multiplication Property of Equality.
4. $a^2 + b^2 = cp + cq = c(p + q)$ — Addition Property; Distributive Property.
blocks.a: The Pythagorean theorem holds for every right triangle.

blocks.name: pythagoras
blocks.cap: The area proof you saw before. Two very different arguments, the same theorem.

blocks.html: In a right triangle, $a^2 = cq$ and $b^2 = cp$ (each leg squared is the hypotenuse times the adjacent piece). Adding them gives $a^2 + b^2 = c(p + q) = c^2$.

blocks.title: The pieces add up
blocks.q: In a right triangle the altitude splits the hypotenuse $c = 10$ into $p = 6.4$ and $q = 3.6$. Find $a$ and $b$, and check $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

blocks.html: The converse. If $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ in a triangle, it is a right triangle. Build a right triangle with legs $a$ and $b$; its hypotenuse is $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = c$. The two triangles are congruent by SSS, so the original angle opposite $c$ is a right angle too.

blocks.title: Using the converse
blocks.q: Is a triangle with sides $7$, $24$ and $25$ a right triangle?
blocks.a: Yes, the angle opposite the side of length $25$ is a right angle.

blocks.html: Adding the wrong squares. The hypotenuse is always the longest side and sits alone on one side of the equation. For sides $5$, $12$, $13$: $5^2 + 12^2 = 13^2$, not $5^2 + 13^2 = 12^2$.

blocks.html: Two right triangles show up so often that their side ratios are worth knowing by heart. Both come straight from the Pythagorean theorem of Proving the Pythagorean Theorem with Similarity, and their answers use the simplified square roots from Simplifying Square Roots.

45-45-90: cut a square with side $s$ along a diagonal. Each half is an isosceles right triangle with legs $s$, so its hypotenuse is $\sqrt{s^2 + s^2} = \sqrt{2s^2} = s\sqrt{2}$.
30-60-90: cut an equilateral triangle with side $2s$ by its altitude. Each half has angles $30^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$, hypotenuse $2s$, and shorter leg $s$ (half of the base). The longer leg is $\sqrt{(2s)^2 - s^2} = \sqrt{3s^2} = s\sqrt{3}$.

Since $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ is between 1 and 2, $s\sqrt{3}$ is the middle side, across from $60^\circ$.

blocks.html: Take any right triangle with an acute angle of $35^\circ$. Every other right triangle with a $35^\circ$ angle is similar to it, by Proving AA Similarity. Similar triangles have proportional sides, so the ratio of any two sides is the same in all of them. Each ratio depends only on the angle, and that is why we can give the ratios names. You saw exact cases in 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 Triangles.
From an acute angle $A$ of a right triangle, the hypotenuse is across from the right angle, the opposite leg is across from $A$, and the adjacent leg is the leg that helps form $A$.

$$\sin A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$ $$\cos A = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$ $$\tan A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$$ (SOH-CAH-TOA). Each ratio depends only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle.

blocks.cap: Change the size: the sides change, but the three ratios do not. Change the angle: the ratios change. Switch to angle $B$: opposite and adjacent trade places.

blocks.html: Why can the ratio not depend on size? Scale the triangle by $k$: the opposite side and the hypotenuse both get multiplied by $k$, and $\frac{k \cdot \text{opp}}{k \cdot \text{hyp}} = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$. The $k$ cancels.
